title: Professional governance: Existing duties need active AI scrutiny
desc: Treats accountability, disclosure and AI-specific regulation as contested extensions of competence rather than blanket reliability rules.

kps.k: The cluster frames legal AI adoption as an institutional responsibility, not simply a choice between automation and professional preservation.
kps.d: The central proposition is that AI can improve legal work only if lawyers, courts, educators and professional bodies build the competence and governance needed to use it responsibly. Ambrogi’s December 2025 account characterises AI as emerging infrastructure; the IBA advocates augmentation rather than replacement. These are strategic assessments, not evidence that adoption is universal or displacement impossible. ABA task-force reports combine recommendations, reported research and contributor forecasts; their authors expressly disclaim approved ABA-policy status, which remains distinct from adopted resolutions and Formal Opinion 512.

qs.q: The goal is to enhance legal expertise, to give lawyers new tools and added value, not to replace them.
qs.a: The Future is Now: Artificial Intelligence and the Legal Profession · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: They have not been reviewed or approved by the House of Delegates or the Board of Governors of the American Bar Association and, accordingly, should not be construed as representing the position of the Association or any of its entities.
qs.a: Addressing the Legal Challenges of AI: Year 2 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Existing professional duties supply the main ethical foundation, while practical compliance requires active scrutiny of tools and outputs.
kps.d: ABA Formal Opinion 512 identifies competence, confidentiality, communication, supervision, candor, meritorious claims and reasonable fees. New Jersey’s guidance likewise treats core duties as unchanged. Pennsylvania and Philadelphia’s committees make verification substantive: lawyers must check whether authorities support the propositions attributed to them, not merely whether citations exist. Kentucky and the USPTO stress provider data handling and third-party confidentiality risks. The CBA argues that consent alone does not discharge risk-management responsibilities. These materials apply jurisdiction-specific obligations and guidance; they do not create one globally binding AI code.

qs.q: When         citing legal authorities such as case law, statutes, regulations, or scholarly articles, lawyers         should verify that the citations accurately reflect the content they are referencing.
qs.a: Joint Formal Opinion 2024-200 — Ethical Issues Regarding the Use of Artificial Intelligence · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: The Ethics Committee has issued Ethics Opinions discussing the ever-changing environment of technology and its application to the Rules, and many of these Opinions are applicable to AI.7 In addition to the guidance provided by these Opinions, we caution lawyers that before using an AI product they review the provider’s privacy policies and its disclaimers in handling client and attorney information.
qs.a: Ethics Opinion KBA E-457 — The Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: The principal regulatory disagreement concerns how much AI-specific intervention existing duties need.
kps.d: Browning favors education and supervision over additional regulation, while appended NYSBA Trusts and Estates Law Section comments favor stable, technology-neutral obligations over frequently revised guidance. By contrast, the IBA recommends reviewing conduct rules and commentary; NYSBA’s task force proposes more explicit technological-competence expectations. The Promise and the Peril of the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Litigation argues that explicit rules also communicate expectations and supports mandatory professional development if voluntary training falls short. Strong goes further, calling incremental changes inadequate to protect autonomy and creativity, although the supplied abstract does not explain her proposed institutional redesign.

qs.q: A better approach would be to address technology                 globally, by focusing on the obligations of the attorney rather than the specific                 technology being employed at the moment.
qs.a: Report and Recommendations of the New York State Bar Association Task Force on Artificial Intelligence (April 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: However, a clear, written rule is not just about imposing an ethical requirement; it is also about communicating the requirement to lawyers.
qs.a: The Promise and the Peril of the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Litigation · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Disclosure remains contested even where human accountability commands broad support.
kps.d: The reported Nigerian guidelines recommend client disclosure and informed consent, and the IBA recommends explaining the scope and type of AI use. Court-filing disclosure raises a different dispute: Browning argues that Rule 11 already establishes responsibility, while NYSBA questions work-product implications and wording that could sweep in established non-generative tools. GenAI Trends reports that the Fifth Circuit abandoned its proposed disclosure rule while retaining existing accuracy requirements. Conrad’s account of federal judicial guidance recommends considering disclosure in context, not a blanket mandate. Opposition to extra certifications therefore does not imply opposition to verification.

qs.q: -  Be transparent with Clients, disclose their use of AI tools to clients, and obtain informed consent before proceeding.
qs.a: Nigerian Bar Association Launches New Technology Guidelines for Legal Practice · Market & press · 2024

qs.q: •   Might the use of the term “artificial intelligence” (rather than generative AI) sweep                 into a disclosure obligation much more than generative AI?
qs.a: Report and Recommendations of the New York State Bar Association Task Force on Artificial Intelligence (April 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Performance evidence supports task-specific use, not blanket claims of reliability or transformation.
kps.d: Thinking Like a Lawyer reports randomized trials involving upper-level law students: GPT-4 accelerated four tasks by approximately 5–38% without statistically significant quality improvement. Later reasoning and retrieval-augmented tools improved speed on five of six assignments, but neither improved speed or quality on NDA drafting; o1-preview improved quality on several other assignments. Separately, an advisor contribution in the ABA Year 1 report reports 17–33% hallucination rates on a particular challenging query dataset. Sanctions incidents establish consequences of improper reliance, not model-wide error rates. These distinctions support testing specific tools and tasks, followed by human verification, rather than treating vendor promises or successful demonstrations as general validation.

qs.q: Particularly strong support for this conclusion comes from two recent randomized controlled trials, in which upper-level law students were tasked with completing a diverse set of realistic lawyering tasks, either with or without the assistance of AI.
qs.a: Thinking Like a Lawyer in the Age of Generative AI: Cognitive Limits on AI Adoption Among Lawyers · Academia · 2025

qs.q: In one study, we documented that hallucinations with legal AI providers range from 17% to 33% in a benchmark dataset of realistic and challenging queries (e.g., bar exam and appellate litigation questions).
qs.a: ABA Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence — Year 1 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law (August 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Operational governance must turn ethical principles into enforceable routines and measurable deployment decisions.
kps.d: NYSBA’s 2025 access-to-justice committee recommends policies before deployment, supervised internal pilots, success metrics, audit trails, authoritative grounding and documented ethics checks. The ABA Year 2 report highlights a further gap: developers must actually implement quality-assessment standards. The soft-law analysis identifies procurement relationships, audits, certification, insurers, funders and liability as possible indirect enforcement mechanisms, not proven solutions. The Victorian census report adds that enterprise AI policies can conflict with lawyers’ professional obligations, particularly outside traditional firms. Practical governance therefore needs clear responsibility, vendor scrutiny and continuing review rather than a policy document alone.

qs.q: To do that, the following principles should guide every step:                                                    9 ^LArtificial Intelligence and Access to Justice in 2025     •   Lead with Policy and Governance, Not Experimentation        Before deploying tools, organizations should adopt plain-language AI policies that define        permitted uses, prohibited practices, and accountability measures.
qs.a: Report and Recommendations on Artificial Intelligence and Access to Justice in 2025 · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: That challenge   – achieving actual adoption of good assessment standards – has generated little discussion   to date and needs attention now to ensure prudent implementation of AI to address   inequities in access to justice.
qs.a: Addressing the Legal Challenges of AI: Year 2 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Unequal institutional capacity qualifies claims that AI has already become routine legal infrastructure.
kps.d: The IBA’s 2024 investigation reports more sophisticated integration in larger firms and predominantly internal uses overall, but its implementation-focused research and larger-firm interviews limit profession-wide inference. NYSBA’s February–April 2025 survey collected 206 responses: nearly nine in ten respondents reported no or slight use, despite substantial motivation and organizational openness. Its committee interprets this as a support gap. Licensing costs, secure infrastructure, technical staffing and training emerge as practical barriers. These findings concern different populations and measures; they are not a common adoption trend series. Ambrogi’s and Harris’s accounts of institutional reports do not independently replicate their underlying findings.

qs.q: The research focused on private practitioners who are already in the implementation stage, revealing the main challenges they have faced and how they have addressed them.
qs.a: The Future is Now: Artificial Intelligence and the Legal Profession · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: In the statewide survey of legal aid professionals, nearly nine in ten reported they were either not using AI or using it only slightly in their work, yet about half said they were moderately or more motivated to use it, and nearly two-thirds believed their organizations were open to AI.
qs.a: Report and Recommendations on Artificial Intelligence and Access to Justice in 2025 · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Access-to-justice benefits depend on affordability, service quality and consumer protection, not productivity alone.
kps.d: The ABA identifies two pathways: expanding legal-aid and pro bono capacity, and supplying understandable assistance directly to people with civil legal problems. Reported use cases and hearing testimony demonstrate applications and perceived benefits, not quantified reductions in unmet need. The Victorian census report asks whether efficiency gains reach clients through affordability, accessibility or quality. NYSBA’s 2025 committee recommends delaying direct-to-client tools until governance and evaluation systems work, then providing human escalation, multilingual access and offline alternatives. Its incremental review of unauthorized-practice restrictions contrasts sharply with an annexed witness’s abolition proposal; that proposal is not the committee’s position.

qs.q: It described the potential for generative AI to improve access to justice in two ways:  1.by increasing the efficiency and productivity of legal services and pro bono lawyers, so that    they can assist many more people with higher levels of service; and  2.by making accurate, usable, and understandable legal information and assistance easily    available to individuals with civil legal problems.
qs.a: Addressing the Legal Challenges of AI: Year 2 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Whether efficiency improvements translate to enhanced affordability, accessibility, or quality for clients, or remain captured elsewhere, has significant implications for the profession’s role in facilitating access to justice.
qs.a: Generative AI Use in the Legal Profession: Findings from the 2025 Victorian Lawyer Census · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Courts distinguish useful administrative assistance from delegation of adjudicative responsibility.
kps.d: Conrad’s October 2025 letter describes temporary federal guidance that permits experimentation while cautioning against delegating decision-making and requiring independent review of outputs. COSCA recommends dedicated multidisciplinary taskforces because AI affects evidence, pleadings, personnel, data and litigant assistance, not merely IT systems. Deepfake authentication presents a separate challenge from verifying AI-written legal analysis: the ABA Year 1 report recounts Grimm and Grossman’s view that existing admissibility rules can suffice with procedural safeguards, while Conrad reports ongoing consideration of evidence-rule amendments. These materials document recommendations and policy development, not demonstrated governance effectiveness.

qs.q: The guidance aims to allow for the use of and experimentation with AI tools while preserving the integrity and independence of the federal courts and the judicial process.
qs.a: Letter from AO Director Robert J. Conrad Jr. to Senate Judiciary Chairman Grassley on the federal Judiciary's use of AI (with the AI Task Force interim guidance summary) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: To do this, COSCA recommends that every court establish a taskforce to assist the court in developing a responsive and flexible institutional framework for the use of generative AI in the courts.38  A taskforce that is separate from any existing court technology committee or advisory body on technology is recommended because the questions raised by generative AI are more than technical.
qs.a: Generative AI and the Future of the Courts: Responsibilities and Possibilities · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: AI competence must preserve the human expertise needed to supervise AI, creating a training problem that output checking alone cannot solve.
kps.d: The IBA recommends continuing to teach juniors work that AI can perform so they develop expertise for senior roles. Mary Smith raises a similar concern through a practitioner anecdote. Artificial Intelligence and Human Legal Reasoning warns of weakened reasoning but acknowledges limited direct legal-sector evidence and relies partly on experiments outside law. Thinking Like a Lawyer tentatively recommends matching use to expertise and task complexity. Educational responses include source reading, deliberate challenge of AI answers, controlled assessments and selective experimentation. The repeatedly cited ABA survey of 29 responding schools documents curricular activity, not the effectiveness of those approaches or independent confirmations across publications.

qs.q: Law firms also need to continue training younger     associates on legal work that may be carried out by AI, which allows them to have well-rooted expertise     when they reach senior roles.
qs.a: The Future is Now: Artificial Intelligence and the Legal Profession · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Over the long term, such gaps could translate into diminished professional capacity in settings where AI is unavailable, constrained, or simply less helpful.45      Although there is limited empirical evidence regarding these potentially negative consequences of AI use in the legal setting, there is mounting evidence demonstrating that it exists in other settings.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and Human Legal Reasoning · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Adaptive coordination is the dominant institutional response, but its effectiveness and the allocation of liability remain unresolved.
kps.d: The ABA plans continuing coordination through its Center for Innovation; COSCA advocates court taskforces; the IBA recommends cross-border knowledge-sharing and adaptable frameworks. California’s 2026 guidance explicitly adds agentic AI, illustrating how greater autonomy changes supervision questions without eliminating professional duties. The IBA’s regulatory questionnaire records differing preferences for comprehensive, moderate and light-touch regulation, rather than consensus on intensity. Ambrogi reports the task force’s prediction that common-law litigation may allocate responsibility among developers, deployers and users. Calls for international cooperation and warnings about more powerful systems remain proposals and forecasts, not evidence that institutions have resolved these challenges.

qs.q: As the AI Task Force concludes at the end of the 2024–2025 bar year, the ABA Center for Innovation will begin implementing strategic goals shaped by the AI Task Force findings and recommendations over the past two years.
qs.a: Addressing the Legal Challenges of AI: Year 2 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Emphasise the importance of stable yet       flexible regulatory frameworks that can adapt to the evolving nature of AI technology while protecting       legal and ethical standards.
qs.a: The Future is Now: Artificial Intelligence and the Legal Profession · Regulators & courts · 2024

vlens.an: The curated legal-tech-vendor sources do not present a single position. Future Ready Lawyer 2026 supports the proposition’s core augmentation model by making continuous human supervision a condition of AI-enabled productivity and by advocating practical AI-literacy development. The 2025 Legal Trends Report instead redirects attention toward changing client behaviour, market expectations, growth and the opportunity to redefine practice; it does not reject professional governance, but provides no corresponding account of verification, disclosure, accountability or tool scrutiny. Thus, the internal variation is primarily one of priority rather than a direct dispute: one source foregrounds competence and human oversight, while the other foregrounds commercial adaptation. Both rely substantially on predictions, recommendations or high-level claims rather than detailed empirical evidence, so neither establishes that the anticipated transformation or benefits have occurred.

qs.q: Law firms will need to      stay abreast of these shifting market dynamics, as they’ll influence what      potential clients look for in a lawyer.
qs.a: 2025 Legal Trends Report · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

vlens.an: Across this curated set, the academia-and-research voice accepts the proposition that legal AI remains subject to professional duties and requires active, human scrutiny. It materially develops that proposition in several ways: randomized studies support task-specific rather than blanket assessments of performance; competence is defined in operational terms such as understanding a tool’s functioning, suitability, limitations and mitigability of risks; and legal education is assigned a continuing role in teaching verification, selective use and preservation of independent reasoning. Other sources extend governance toward effectiveness testing, institutional review, human-centred access-to-justice design and cross-border coordination. The common rationale is that AI offers plausible or demonstrated efficiency benefits but produces uneven results and risks—including fabricated authorities, confidentiality problems, sycophancy and possible erosion of professional judgment—that prevent unqualified reliance. Material internal variation concerns the required intensity and locus of intervention: Browning favours education, supervision and existing accountability rules over additional disclosure regulation; other authors support explicit competence rules, mandatory training or revisable institutional controls; Strong redirects more sharply toward fundamental reform of the profession and legal education. Several excerpts provide only research agendas, outlines, references or institutional context, so their positions remain indeterminate. These differences describe the selected sources and should not be read as showing how prevalent any view is within academia or research generally.

qs.q: Consequently, competence entails understanding how a particular technology functions and its suitability for the planned task, including risks and limitations, and how they can or cannot be ameliorated.210 Ideally competence would be supported by firms’ policies, due diligence on AI
qs.a: The Promise and the Peril of the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Litigation · Academia · 2025

vlens.an:
The curated regulators, courts and professional-body sources accept the proposition’s core: existing professional duties remain the foundation for legal AI use, but compliance requires active scrutiny rather than trust in apparently reliable output. They materially develop that proposition by translating competence, confidentiality, candor, supervision and client protection into institutional mechanisms: verification of outputs and authorities, provider and data-handling review, training, approved-tool policies, staged pilots, audit trails, task-specific benchmarking, lifecycle assessment, multidisciplinary court taskforces and continuing policy review. Courts additionally preserve human accountability by distinguishing administrative assistance from delegation of adjudication.

Their common reasoning is that AI may improve efficiency, service delivery and access to justice, but can also fabricate authorities, expose confidential information, introduce bias or conflicts, and encourage overreliance. Benefits are generally framed as potential or task-dependent; guidance documents and institutional actions are not treated as proof of performance or governance effectiveness. Several sources also identify unequal institutional capacity, especially across firm sizes, legal-aid providers and non-traditional practice settings, as a reason governance must include training, infrastructure and vendor controls.

Material variation concerns the extent and form of AI-specific intervention. Some sources treat existing, technology-neutral duties as largely sufficient; others favour amendments to competence commentary, updated conduct rules, dedicated AI bodies or targeted legislation where evidence reveals gaps. Disclosure is similarly context-sensitive: some recommend client disclosure, while judicial guidance and NYSBA materials question blanket filing certifications and imprecise definitions that could encompass established non-generative tools. Operational ambition also differs, ranging from high-level reminders of existing duties to detailed pre-deployment controls and lifecycle governance. Access-to-justice sources go further on equity and client-facing safeguards, while court sources emphasise judicial independence, evidentiary authenticity and non-delegation. These differences refine implementation rather than displace the principal proposition, and the curated selection should not be read as representative of all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: That means enterprise-grade tools with zero        data retention, retrieval-augmented grounding to authoritative sources, mandatory human        verification, and documented ethics checks.
qs.a: Report and Recommendations on Artificial Intelligence and Access to Justice in 2025 · Regulators & courts · 2026

vlens.an: The selected traditional-law-firm sources support the proposition that legal AI adoption should proceed through active professional oversight rather than assumptions of blanket reliability. Their common rationale is that AI may augment legal work and improve service, but lawyers remain accountable under existing duties and need clearer governance, competence and verification practices. There is material variation over implementation: “Ten AI Predictions for 2026” strongly favours formal institutional policies and depicts disclosure and verification orders as part of the emerging infrastructure, whereas “GenAI Trends in the Legal Profession in 2024” is more receptive to technology-neutral regulation, highlighting the Fifth Circuit’s conclusion that existing filing-accuracy rules can cover AI without a separate disclosure requirement. The latter also makes more optimistic forecasts about adoption and improving accuracy; these predictions do not undermine its continuing emphasis on human responsibility. Because these are curated sources, their alignment should not be treated as representative of traditional law firms generally.

qs.q: Informal policies and ad hoc experimentation no longer suffice.
qs.a: Ten AI Predictions for 2026: What Leading Analysts Say Legal Teams Should Expect · Law firms · 2025

qs.q: The court agreed that existing court rules that require lawyers to certify the accuracy of court filings were sufficient to encompass AI.
qs.a: GenAI Trends in the Legal Profession in 2024 · Law firms · 2024

vlens.an:
This curated set of market-analysis, consultancy and press sources supports the proposition that legal AI adoption requires active professional and institutional governance rather than uncritical reliance on the technology. The common reasoning is that lawyers and judges remain accountable for AI-assisted work, so they must understand tool limitations, verify outputs, preserve confidentiality and exercise independent professional judgment. The sources also frame AI capability and organisational readiness as increasingly important professional competencies.

There is material variation in depth and emphasis. The report on the Nigerian Bar Association guidelines is prescriptive at the practitioner level, including verification, supervision, confidentiality, client disclosure and informed consent; its disclosure position is one side of the cluster’s acknowledged debate, not a universal rule. LawCPD offers only broad claims that generative AI and digital diligence are becoming necessary, without supplying the survey results or operational governance detail needed to substantiate those claims. Ambrogi develops the most institutional account, extending scrutiny across the AI lifecycle and highlighting courts, legal education, access to justice, unequal implementation capacity and unresolved liability. However, much of that account reports task-force recommendations, examples and forecasts rather than independently established outcomes. Claims that AI is already everyday reality or core infrastructure should therefore not be generalized across the profession from these selected sources.

qs.q: Critically review outputs generated by AI tools before relying on them in client work.
qs.a: Nigerian Bar Association Launches New Technology Guidelines for Legal Practice · Market & press · 2024

qs.q: Drawing on frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the Task Force emphasizes the need for organizational strategies that address data quality, transparency, accountability and human oversight across the AI lifecycle.
qs.a: ABA Task Force: AI Has Moved from Experiment to Infrastructure for the Legal Profession · Market & press · 2025

elens.an: The 2015–2022 sources accept the proposition’s core: legal AI should augment parts of legal practice only under continuing human and institutional scrutiny. Their common reasoning is that AI’s effects vary by task and professional context, so lawyers must retain the competence to supervise, question and interpret outputs rather than assume general reliability. The period materially develops the proposition through the soft-law source’s concrete framework for task-specific effectiveness testing and indirect enforcement via internal governance, auditing, certification, professional bodies, market mechanisms, regulators and liability. There is meaningful internal variation: “Becoming the AI-Enhanced Lawyer” primarily offers a broad prediction of partial automation coupled with lawyer oversight and warns against profession-wide generalisation, whereas the soft-law analysis focuses on institutional controls and vendor governance. The latter presents possible mechanisms, however, not empirical evidence that they work. These curated sources therefore anticipate and extend the cluster’s governance framework without resolving the later disputes over disclosure, regulatory intensity or demonstrated effectiveness.

qs.q: For the legal profession in the 21st century, AI will change the practice of law by automating parts of the lawyering process and lawyers will need to be able to use those new tools to enhance their professional offering, but also supervise, question and interpret AI.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and the Legal Profession: Becoming the AI-Enhanced Lawyer · Academia · 2019

qs.q: Soft Law Governance of Artificial Intelligence             market forces, labeling, professional journals, FTC                     Academics and organizations could develop and            enforcement, and liability.
qs.a: Evaluating Artificial Intelligence for Legal Services: Can ‘Soft Law’ Lead to Enforceable Standards for Effectiveness? · Academia · 2021

elens.an: The 2023–2024 “generative shock” sources accept the proposition’s core and materially develop its practical meaning. Across this curated set, ethics opinions, court guidance, bar reports and scholarship generally treat generative AI as potentially useful but fallible: existing duties of competence, confidentiality, candor, communication and supervision continue to govern, while responsible use requires verification of outputs, scrutiny of provider data practices, training and retained human judgment. Several sources go further by proposing concrete institutional mechanisms—standing taskforces, evolving guidance, expanded technology-competence expectations, transparency and task-specific benchmarking, lifecycle impact assessments, and cross-border coordination. Internal variation concerns the extent of AI-specific intervention rather than the need for accountability: some favour disclosure, consent and updated conduct rules, while others argue that technology-neutral duties, education and existing filing-certification rules are generally sufficient. Access-to-justice, productivity and transformative benefits are mostly framed as possibilities or forecasts; the limited empirical evidence supports faster completion of some legal tasks, not blanket reliability. Citation-fabrication incidents illustrate the consequences of failed verification but are not measured hallucination rates. These sources are a curated selection and therefore do not establish how prevalent any view was across the profession.

qs.q: Law firms, bar associations, academics, and technology providers must develop transparency and benchmarking requirements to assess the appropriateness, trustworthiness, benefits, and risks of specific AI tools.
qs.a: ABA Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence — Year 1 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law (August 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: The 2025 sources collectively accept the proposition that scaling legal AI requires active scrutiny under continuing professional duties, and they materially develop it into an implementation agenda. Their common reasons are that AI outputs remain fallible and task-dependent; lawyers and judges retain responsibility for AI-assisted work; confidentiality, data handling, supervision and competence require tool-specific assessment; and adoption at institutional scale needs policies, procurement controls, training, auditability, lifecycle oversight and independent human verification. Several sources add concrete extensions: federal Judiciary guidance distinguishes controlled experimentation from delegation of adjudication and treats disclosure as context-dependent; the ABA Task Force report identifies the neglected problem of securing developers’ actual adoption of quality standards and establishes continuing coordination mechanisms; competence scholarship proposes explicit rules or mandatory training where voluntary education is inadequate; and randomized law-student trials support expertise- and task-sensitive deployment rather than blanket reliability claims. Material variation concerns regulatory intensity and emphasis, not the core need for accountability. Some sources favour clearer AI-specific duties and training, while others argue that established ethical frameworks cover many uses but may need supplementation for disruptive applications. Access-to-justice sources stress affordability, quality and consumer protection; market-oriented reporting instead redirects attention toward client expectations and firm growth without substantively addressing verification or governance. Some supplied excerpts contain only research framing, outlines or bibliographies, so their positions remain indeterminate. Claims that AI is becoming infrastructure or will deliver large productivity, contracting or access gains are strategic assessments or forecasts, not proof of universal adoption or measured system-wide outcomes; the curated sources should not be treated as representative of all 2025 legal actors.

qs.q: In particular, we suggest that firms may want to limit AI usage among junior attorneys to specific tasks that do not implicate complex legal reasoning, while encouraging AI usage among more expert lawyers on tasks for which they are well equipped to quickly and accurately evaluate the quality, limitations, and implications of AI-generated materials.
qs.a: Thinking Like a Lawyer in the Age of Generative AI: Cognitive Limits on AI Adoption Among Lawyers · Academia · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources broadly accept the cluster’s principal proposition that existing professional duties remain the foundation for legal-AI use but require active, institutionally organised scrutiny. They materially develop it by extending guidance to agentic AI; specifying governance before deployment, staged pilots, audit trails, authoritative grounding and mandatory human verification; and adapting legal education and workplace training so lawyers retain the substantive expertise needed to supervise AI. Additional extensions include attention to reasoning erosion, uneven organisational capacity, conflicts between enterprise policies and lawyers’ duties, and whether efficiency gains actually improve access to justice. The evidence base varies materially: the NYSBA access-to-justice report and Victorian census provide survey-based or census-based evidence for defined populations, whereas several other sources offer guidance, conference forecasts, expert recommendations or capability claims without detailed supporting results. There is also a significant internal redirection: Strong accepts responsible adoption but argues that incremental adaptation of existing systems is insufficient and calls for fundamental reform of the profession and legal education. The federal-courts survey excerpts provide only institutional context, leaving their substantive position unclear. These differences show variation within this curated set and should not be read as indicating the prevalence of any view across the profession.

qs.q: This 2026 Practical Guidance replaces the 2023 version and, at the request of the California Supreme Court, addresses the unique challenges presented by the use of agentic AI.
qs.a: Practical Guidance for the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2026
